runs.text: A condensed study overview for the

exams. It follows the chapters of the ArchiMate 3.2 course: basic concepts, framework and notation, generic metamodel, relationships, motivation, strategy, the three core layers with physical elements, cross-layer dependencies, implementation and migration, and viewpoints. It ends with naming conventions, common confusions and the exam format.
The orange boxes summarise the points candidates most often get wrong in the exam.
is a visual modelling language with a default set of icons. It is used to describe, analyse and communicate enterprise architectures and how they change over time.
is any collection of organizations with common goals: a whole company or one of its divisions, a government agency, but also a consortium or a supply chain.
(ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010) means the fundamental concepts or properties of a system in its environment, embodied in its elements, relationships and the principles of its design and evolution.
. The architect refines their requirements, builds
showing how they will be met and makes the trade-offs between conflicting concerns visible.
is a formal description of a system, organised so that one can reason about its structure, behavior and evolution.
The language gives a uniform notation for diagrams, viewpoints for selected stakeholders and customization mechanisms. It relates the layers through
(a lower layer serves a higher one) and through

paragraphs.text: A collection of concepts in the context of the ArchiMate language structure.
An element or a relationship. (A junction is a relationship connector, i.e. a concept joining relationships.)
The basic unit of the metamodel: behavior, structure (active / passive), motivation or composite element.
A connection between a source and a target concept. Classified as structural, dependency, dynamic or other.
A concept that joins two or more relationships of the same type (junction).
A level of abstraction at which an enterprise can be modelled.
A classification of elements by layer-independent characteristics related to the concerns of different stakeholders.
A structure or behavior element in one of the core layers.
An element made up of elements from several aspects or layers:
A property attached to an element or a relationship.
The central part of the language: the concepts of the Business, Application and Technology layers (including Physical).
The reference structure for classifying core elements:
A representation of a system from the perspective of related concerns. “What you see.”
A specification of the conventions for a kind of view. “Where you are looking from.”
A stakeholder has a key role in, or concerns about, the system. A concern is an interest that is crucial to them and decides whether the system is acceptable (performance, reliability, security…).
Fulfilment of specified requirements. A conforming implementation meets the conformance clause of the standard.
Elements that perform behavior (actor, component, node…).
Elements that behavior acts on (business object, data object, artifact…).
Context and reasons behind the architecture (goal, requirement…).
Why. Only in the Full Framework.
Strategic direction and choices: capabilities, resources, value streams, courses of action.
Services offered to customers and the processes, roles and actors delivering them.
Application services supporting the business and the applications that realize them.
Processing, storage and communication services, hardware and system software. Physical elements add machines, facilities, distribution networks and material.
Realizing the architecture: work packages, deliverables, plateaus and gaps.
Core Framework = Business, Application, Technology × active structure, behavior, passive structure. Motivation, Strategy and Implementation & Migration are added only by the Full Framework.
Physical elements are not a separate layer but an extension of the Technology Layer.
Colours have no formal meaning. Yellow / blue / green for Business / Application / Technology is only the convention of the examples in the standard.

An external or internal condition that motivates an organization to set goals and make changes.
The result of analysing the state of the enterprise with respect to a driver.
Noun or short sentence: “High complaint rate”.

An end result, effect or consequence of a certain state of affairs.

The relative worth, utility or importance of a concept.
Action or state: “Be sure of delivery”.

paragraphs.text: An asset owned or controlled by an individual or organization.
The only structure element of the strategy layer. Tangible, intangible and human assets. Realized by active and passive structure elements.
An ability that an active structure element (organization, person, system) possesses.
Behavior. Focuses on business outcomes; the name says “what we do”, not “how we do it”.
A sequence of activities that creates an overall result for a customer, stakeholder or end user.
Behavior. Verb–noun in active tense. Typically realized by business processes.
An approach or plan for configuring capabilities and resources to achieve a goal.
Behavior. What the enterprise has decided to do (strategies, tactics).

runs.text: a capability or a value stream. A capability
Capabilities and value streams serve or realize a course of action; a course of action realizes or influences an outcome. Strategy elements can also realize or influence a requirement.
Core elements realize strategy: internal and external behavior elements realize capabilities or value streams; active and passive structure elements realize resources.
A capability describes the enterprise “at rest” (what it can do), a value stream “in motion” (how it creates value).

goes from the more concrete to the more abstract: artifact → data object → business object; artifact → application component.

paragraphs.text: Active and passive structure (actor, role, interface, component, node, business object, data object, material…)
Verb or verb–noun; may contain the word “process”.
Verb ending in “-ing”; a service may contain the word “service”.
The name should clearly indicate a well-defined behavior.
Verb in the simple present tense.
Noun naming the type of hardware / environment.
The name of the file it represents.
Goal qualitatively, outcome as an achieved state.
Capability says “what we do”; value stream verb–noun.
A process has an order of steps and a result. A function groups behavior by competences and resources, without order.
A service is behavior offered externally. An interface is the place (channel) where the service is available; the interface is
An actor is a concrete entity, a role is a responsibility. An actor is assigned to a role, a role to behavior.
Assignment = who performs it or where it runs. Realization = what is the concrete form of a more abstract element.
In a composition a part belongs to only one whole. In an aggregation a part can belong to several wholes.
Triggering = sequence in time. Flow = something is transferred (data, goods, money), without causality.
Serving points to the element that uses the functionality. Access goes from behavior to a passive element.
A goal is an intention, an outcome is an achieved (measurable) result.
A principle applies generally to all systems in a context, a requirement to one specific system.
A driver is a condition that motivates change. An assessment is the result of analysing it.
A capability says what the enterprise can do (strategy). A function says how behavior is organised (operations).
A value stream shows at the strategic level how value is created. A business process realizes it at the operational level.
A business object is a business concept, a data object its logical data, an artifact the physical file. Realization goes bottom-up.
A path is a logical link, a communication network the physical network that realizes it.
A device is hardware, system software a runtime environment, a node a general resource that can be composed of them.
A deliverable is a result of work, a plateau a state of the architecture, a gap the difference between two states.
A view is what you see. A viewpoint is where you look from (the rules by which a view is created).
Knowledge and comprehension: notation, terminology, structure and basic concepts of the language.
In addition, the ability to apply and analyse this knowledge.
